questions.title: How can likelihood of confusion be a 'question of law' if the DuPont factors are treated as factual findings?
questions.question_body: I'm confused by the standard of review section. The Federal Circuit says likelihood of confusion is a question of law, but that the individual DuPont factors are questions of fact reviewed for substantial evidence. In practice, what does that distinction do on appeal from the TTAB? Does the court independently re-weigh the factors once it accepts the Board's fact findings, or is it mostly limited to checking whether the Board applied the correct legal framework?

questions.title: What exactly happens procedurally when an intent-to-use application is opposed after publication?
questions.question_body: Apex filed intent-to-use applications, CC Serve filed a letter of protest during prosecution, the examining attorney still approved the marks for publication, and then CC Serve brought an opposition before the TTAB. I'm not sure I understand the procedural significance of each step. If the examining attorney already allowed publication despite the protest, why doesn't that settle the issue? Is an opposition basically a separate adversarial proceeding where the TTAB can reach a different result based on a fuller record?

questions.title: Why did the Board treat 'credit card services' and 'banking and financing services' as legally identical in part?
questions.question_body: The applicant argued that it doesn't offer credit cards and that CC Serve itself just partners with banks, so I expected the services to be considered related at most. But the Board said the services were 'legally identical, in part' because dictionary definitions of banking and finance can include extending credit through credit cards. How does that work in trademark law? Is the comparison based only on the wording in the registration/application rather than the parties' real-world business models, and is that why Apex's current lack of credit card services did not matter?

questions.title: Why was the Board allowed to interpret the old identification 'credit card services' so broadly after that entry was deleted from the ID Manual?
questions.question_body: The opinion says the old 'credit card services' entry had been deleted from the Trademark ID Manual, so the Board had to determine what the identified services meant. It then included things like issuing cards, processing transactions, monitoring, account management, and access to credit scores. I'm confused about the source of that interpretation. When an old identification is vague or outdated, what legal materials can the TTAB use to define its scope, and how much flexibility does it have in doing so?

questions.title: Why did the Federal Circuit say the TTAB used the wrong scope of comparison under the sixth DuPont factor?
questions.question_body: For the sixth DuPont factor, the Board limited the relevant third-party evidence to Aspire-formative marks used for credit card services and treated Aspire marks used for broader banking or financing services as basically irrelevant. The Federal Circuit said that was legal error because the second factor had already found the parties' services highly similar and partly legally identical. I'm struggling with the doctrinal point here: does the court mean the definition of 'similar goods/services' should stay consistent across DuPont factors unless there's a specific reason to change it? Or is this only about third-party-use evidence of weakness?

questions.title: What is the difference between proving a mark is commercially weak versus conceptually weak under the sixth DuPont factor?
questions.question_body: The opinion says Apex offered third-party Aspire uses to show weakness, and the Board concluded CC Serve had not shown particular commercial strength, but Apex also had not shown the mark was commercially or conceptually weak enough to deserve a narrow scope of protection. I get that third-party use can weaken a mark, but I'm not clear on the two different kinds of weakness here. What evidence goes to commercial weakness versus conceptual weakness, and why would that matter to how much protection the ASPIRE mark gets?

questions.title: Why did the court vacate the first DuPont factor without actually deciding whether ASPIRE and ASPIRE BANK are similar marks?
questions.question_body: The Federal Circuit affirmed the services-similarity factor, vacated the sixth factor, and then also vacated the first factor because changes to the sixth factor could affect commercial strength and therefore commercial impression. I'm having trouble seeing the connection. I thought the first factor was just a side-by-side comparison of the marks' appearance, sound, meaning, and overall impression. How does new evidence or reconsideration of third-party Aspire marks change that analysis, and could the Board still reach the same result on remand?

questions.title: Why were costs awarded to Apex if it only won a vacatur and remand rather than outright registration?
questions.question_body: The disposition says 'affirmed-in-part, vacated-in-part, and remanded,' but then it awards costs to appellant. Since Apex did not fully prevail and the court even affirmed the Board on the second DuPont factor, I'm confused why costs go to Apex. Is the party that secures a vacatur/remand usually treated as the prevailing party for appellate costs, or is there a specific Federal Circuit rule for this situation?
